# Hidetaka Miyazaki — Key Interview Quotes and Insights

## On Fragmented Storytelling and Design Philosophy

> "I don't want to make a game where there's one clear answer. I want the player to piece things together, to form their own interpretation. The fragments are deliberately arranged so that multiple readings are possible, and the 'truth' is something each player arrives at individually."
— Miyazaki, various interviews

> "The item descriptions are not just flavor text. They are the primary storytelling vehicle. Every description is carefully written and placed. If you read them carefully and think about where you found them and who dropped them, a picture emerges. But it's never a complete picture. That's intentional."
— Miyazaki on Elden Ring's narrative approach

> "I don't think of the lore as a puzzle with one solution. It's more like an archaeological site. You dig up fragments and you try to reconstruct what happened, but you'll never have every piece. That incompleteness is part of the experience."
— Miyazaki on environmental storytelling

[Context: Miyazaki has consistently described his narrative philosophy across multiple interviews. The fragmented, indirect storytelling is not a limitation but a deliberate design choice maintained across all FromSoftware Soulsborne titles.]

## On Queen Marika's Motivation

> "Marika's actions — the removal of Destined Death, the exile of the Tarnished, the eventual Shattering — are all connected by a single thread, but I want the player to discover what that thread is. Was she trying to create a perfect world? Was she rebelling against the Greater Will? Was she simply going mad? The evidence supports multiple readings, and I think that's appropriate for a character who is literally two people in one body."
— Miyazaki, discussing Marika/Radagon

> "The relationship between Marika and Radagon is the heart of the story. They are one being with two wills, and the tension between those wills is what drove the Shattering. Marika wanted to break the Ring; Radagon wanted to repair it. They are both right and both wrong."
— Miyazaki on the central conflict

[Context: Miyazaki has been deliberately evasive about providing definitive answers regarding Marika's intent, though he confirms the duality with Radagon is central.]

## On the Nature of the Tarnished

> "The Tarnished are not heroes in the traditional sense. They are people who failed — who were cast out because they were no longer useful. Their return is not triumphant; it's desperate. They come back to a world that rejected them, and they have to decide what to do with it."
— Miyazaki on player character identity

> "I think there's something interesting about playing as someone who has already lost. The Tarnished lost their grace, lost their homeland, lost their purpose. Everything they do in the game is an attempt to reclaim something, but what they reclaim may not be what they lost."
— Miyazaki on the Tarnished's journey

[Context: These quotes inform the game's approach to the player character as a figure defined by loss and exile rather than destiny or heroism.]

## On Why the World Is Ruined

> "The Lands Between were not destroyed by an external force. They were destroyed from within, by the very systems meant to sustain them. The Golden Order created a world of apparent perfection by removing death, by enforcing a rigid hierarchy, by excluding anything that didn't fit. The Shattering is what happens when a system built on exclusion and denial finally collapses under the weight of everything it suppressed."
— Miyazaki on the state of the world

> "Every beautiful thing in the Lands Between has something terrible underneath it. The Erdtree is golden and magnificent, but its roots are diseased. Leyndell is a gorgeous city, but beneath it are sewers full of the cursed and abandoned. This is not accidental. The beauty and the horror are two aspects of the same system."
— Miyazaki on environmental storytelling

[Context: These quotes explain the consistent pattern across the game's locations: surface beauty concealing institutional cruelty.]

## On the Endings

> "I wanted each ending to feel like a genuine choice with genuine consequences. None of them are simply 'good' or 'bad.' Each one addresses a real problem in the world but creates new problems in doing so. The player has to decide which set of problems they prefer."
— Miyazaki on the multiple endings

> "Ranni's ending is interesting because it's the most complete departure from the existing system. She doesn't fix the Golden Order; she replaces it. Whether that's better or worse is for the player to decide."
— Miyazaki on Ranni's Age of Stars

> "The Frenzied Flame ending is the most extreme option. It's the answer of someone who looks at a broken world and decides the only solution is to unmake it entirely. I don't think it's the 'wrong' answer, but I do think the game makes it clear that it's the most destructive one."
— Miyazaki on the Lord of Frenzied Flame ending

[Context: Miyazaki has maintained that no ending is canonically "correct," though the DLC's existence implies the base game endings precede its events.]

## On Collaboration with George R.R. Martin

> "Martin-san created the overarching mythology — the world's deep history, the pantheon, the family relationships among the demigods. I then took that mythology and shattered it, literally and figuratively. The game you play takes place in the ruins of the story he wrote."
— Miyazaki on the GRRM collaboration

> "His contribution was the 'mythos' — the foundational stories that existed before the game begins. The wars, the betrayals, the family dynamics. I was responsible for the game's present tense: what the player encounters, how the world looks now, what happened after the Shattering."
— Miyazaki on the division of creative labor

[Context: The collaboration is frequently mischaracterized as Martin writing the game's story. In reality, Martin provided the backstory and cosmogony, while Miyazaki and the FromSoftware team built the in-game world and narrative.]

## On Difficulty and Accessibility

> "The difficulty is part of the narrative. When a boss defeats you twenty times and you finally succeed, that struggle becomes part of your story. The game is hard because the Lands Between are hard. The Tarnished suffer, and the player suffers with them. Removing that suffering would remove the meaning."
— Miyazaki on difficulty as storytelling

> "Elden Ring's open world was our answer to the accessibility question. If a boss is too hard, you can go somewhere else, get stronger, and come back. The freedom to choose your path is the accessibility feature. We didn't make the challenges easier; we gave you more ways to approach them."
— Miyazaki on Elden Ring's open-world approach to difficulty

[Context: These quotes address the long-running discourse about FromSoftware game difficulty.]

## On the DLC (Shadow of the Erdtree)

> "The Land of Shadow is the other side of the Erdtree — literally and metaphorically. Everything the Golden Order buried, denied, or cast away ended up there. The DLC is about confronting what the main game's world tried to hide."
— Miyazaki on Shadow of the Erdtree's themes

> "Miquella is the most important character in the DLC, but not in the way players might expect. His story is about the cost of good intentions and what happens when someone who genuinely wants to save the world discovers the price that requires."
— Miyazaki on Miquella's role in the DLC

[Context: These quotes establish the DLC as thematically essential, not supplementary — it explores the Golden Order's shadow side that the base game only hinted at.]
